newsitem.title: UK: PPL to test cystic fibrosis drug in people.
newsitem.headline: PPL to test cystic fibrosis drug in people.

text.p: The scientists who created the first cloned adult mammal -- Dolly the sheep -- said on Wednesday they would start phase II clinical trials of a genetically engineered protein for cystic fibrosis.
PPL Therapeutics will test the protein, produced by genetically engineered sheep in their milk, at Papworth Hospital in Cambridge.
Dr Ron James, managing director of PPL, said Britain's Medicines Control Agency had granted a Clinical Trials Exemption certificate for the tests in 12 volunteers with cystic fibrosis.
"We believe it is the first time the UK authorities have examined a transgenically derived product and it is a significant milestone for PPL," he said in a statement.

The protein, alpha-antitrypsin (AAT), is a human protein. The sheep bred at PPL's joint laboratory with the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh have been bred to express human genes that "code" for production of the protein.

They currently do this by injecting the DNA for the gene into the nucleus of a fertilised sheep embryo. The process is hit-and-miss, which is why PPL is working on clones -- they could breed many twins of a successfully engineered animal, all producing the protein in their milk.
Phase I trials in 40 volunteers showed AAT is safe and well-tolerated in people. The phase II trials will look at efficacy and try to help home in on what the best dose would be.
Cystic fibrosis, the most common genetic disease among people of European origin, is deadly and there is no cure. Victims suffer lung and intestinal damage and usually die before they are 30.
AAT is a treatment for the symptoms of cystic fibrosis, not a cure. It helps correct the lung tissue breakdown.
"This could potentially be very exciting news for cystic fibrosis sufferers," said Dr Diana Bilton, who will lead the trial at Papworth.
A later study will examine the effects of the drug on 60 CF patients over four weeks. This will be followed by a six month trial involving 160 patients at up to 20 centres.
